stem: Tern Logistics sues Ames Freight for breach of a contract under which Ames was to deliver goods to a warehouse owned by Corbin, and asks for orders directing both delivery by Ames and acceptance of the goods by the warehouse. Corbin is not a party. The court finds that, without Corbin, it cannot give Tern and Ames complete relief between themselves. Corbin can be served, and joining Corbin would not affect jurisdiction or venue.
ask: Which provision makes Corbin a person who must be joined?

options.t: Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(i), because Corbin's ability to protect its interest may be impaired.
options.why: Rule 19(a)(1)(B) applies only to a person who claims an interest relating to the subject of the action; Corbin has claimed none.

options.t: Rule 19(b), because the court must decide in equity and good conscience whether to proceed.
options.why: Rule 19(b) applies only after a required person cannot be joined; Corbin can be joined, so the factors are not reached.

options.t: Rule 19(a)(1)(A), because without Corbin the court cannot accord complete relief among existing parties.
options.why: Correct. The court's finding that it cannot give Tern and Ames complete relief is exactly the Rule 19(a)(1)(A) test.

options.t: Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(ii), because Ames faces a risk of inconsistent obligations.
options.why: Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(ii) needs a claimed interest and a substantial risk of double or inconsistent obligations; neither is described.

explain: Rule 19(a)(1)(A) requires joinder of a person who can be served and whose joinder will not defeat jurisdiction when, in that person's absence, the court cannot accord complete relief among existing parties. The court so found as to Corbin. Subparagraph (B) turns on a claimed interest, and Rule 19(b) is reached only when a required person cannot be joined.

cites.quote: in that person's absence, the court cannot accord complete relief among existing parties

stem: Vega sues Hart Realty, asking the court to declare void Hart's sale of a lakefront parcel to Ostrom, who holds the deed and claims to own the parcel. Ostrom is not named as a party. The court agrees it could give Vega and Hart complete relief between themselves. Ostrom can be served, and joining Ostrom would not affect jurisdiction or venue.
ask: Must Ostrom be joined?

options.t: No. Rule 19(a)(1)(A) is the only ground for required joinder, and complete relief is possible without Ostrom.
options.why: Subparagraphs (A) and (B) are alternatives joined by 'or'; satisfying (B) is enough even when (A) is not met.

options.t: No. Only a plaintiff decides whom to sue, so the court cannot add Ostrom.
options.why: Rule 19(a)(2) provides that if a person has not been joined as required, the court must order that the person be made a party.

options.t: Yes, but only after Ostrom moves to intervene under Rule 24.
options.why: Rule 19(a) imposes no intervention precondition; the court itself must order joinder under Rule 19(a)(2).

options.t: Yes. Ostrom claims an interest in the parcel, and a judgment voiding the sale in Ostrom's absence may impair Ostrom's ability to protect it.
options.why: Correct. Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(i): a claimed interest plus a practical risk of impairment.

explain: Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(i) requires joinder of a person who claims an interest relating to the subject of the action and is so situated that deciding the case without that person may, as a practical matter, impair or impede the person's ability to protect it. Ostrom holds the deed and claims ownership, so a judgment voiding the sale could do exactly that. Rule 19(a)(1)(A) is an alternative, not a prerequisite.

stem: Quincy sues Pelham Mutual, an insurer, to collect $100,000 in life-policy proceeds as the policy's beneficiary. Rask also claims to be the beneficiary and has told Pelham so in writing. Rask is not a party, can be served, and could be joined without affecting jurisdiction or venue. Pelham argues that Rask must be joined to protect Pelham itself, not just Rask.
ask: Which provision speaks to the risk Pelham, an existing party, faces if Rask is absent?

options.t: Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(i), which protects Rask's ability to protect his own interest.
options.why: Subparagraph (i) addresses harm to the absent person; the stem asks about the risk to an existing party.

options.t: Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(ii), which covers a substantial risk of double or inconsistent obligations to an existing party.
options.why: Correct. Pelham could owe the proceeds to Quincy and again to Rask.

options.t: Rule 19(b)(1), which asks about prejudice to the existing parties.
options.why: Rule 19(b) is reached only when a required person cannot be joined; here Rask can be joined.

options.t: Rule 19(c), which makes Rask a required party once Pelham pleads his name.
options.why: Rule 19(c) is a pleading duty to state names and reasons; it does not make anyone required.

explain: Rule 19(a)(1)(B)(ii) covers a person who claims an interest and is so situated that disposing of the action in that person's absence may leave an existing party subject to a substantial risk of double, multiple, or otherwise inconsistent obligations because of the interest. Pelham could be ordered to pay Quincy and then Rask. Subparagraph (i), by contrast, concerns harm to the absent person.

cites.quote: leave an existing party subject to a substantial risk of incurring double, multiple, or otherwise inconsistent obligations because of the interest

stem: Dunmore sues Eller Co. in federal court. The court finds that Fisk must be joined if feasible and orders Fisk made a party. Once joined, Fisk objects that venue is improper as to Fisk. The court agrees that joining Fisk makes venue improper.
ask: What does Rule 19(a)(3) require the court to do?

options.t: Dismiss Fisk as a party.
options.why: Correct. Rule 19(a)(3): if a joined party objects to venue and joinder would make venue improper, the court must dismiss that party.

options.t: Overrule the objection, because an order of joinder under Rule 19(a)(2) displaces venue objections.
options.why: Rule 19(a)(3) expressly gives a joined party's venue objection effect.

options.t: Dismiss the entire action immediately, because a required person is missing.
options.why: Rule 19(a)(3) dismisses only the party; whether the action proceeds is Rule 19(b)'s separate question.

options.t: Treat the objection as waived, because Fisk did not raise it before being ordered joined.
options.why: Rule 19(a)(3) covers a joined party who objects; it contains no waiver-by-joinder rule.

explain: Rule 19(a)(3) says that if a joined party objects to venue and the joinder would make venue improper, the court must dismiss that party. Fisk objected after being joined, and the court agreed that venue would be improper. Dismissing the whole action is not what subdivision (a)(3) commands; whether to proceed without Fisk is for Rule 19(b).

cites.quote: If a joined party objects to venue and the joinder would make venue improper, the court must dismiss that party.

stem: Hale Dairy sues Pruitt Farms over a milk-supply contract. Ward, a required person, cannot be joined. The judge asks what favors letting the case go forward. The court can write a judgment that binds only Hale and Pruitt and leaves Ward's separate contract untouched. Hale has no other court in which it could bring this claim.
ask: What is Hale's best argument that the action should proceed without Ward?

options.t: Ward refuses to join, so Rule 19(a)(2) lets the court proceed without Ward.
options.why: Rule 19(a)(2) concerns ordering joinder; it does not authorize proceeding when joinder fails.

options.t: Hale chose its parties, and Rule 19 gives the plaintiff the final say on whether to proceed.

options.why: Rule 19(d) only makes the rule subject to Rule 23 for class actions.

The decision belongs to the court, not to Hale.

shaping the relief

stem: Lund sues Moss Builders for breach of a construction contract. Lund knows that Nye, a subcontractor who claims an interest in the same contract payments, is a person who is required to be joined if feasible. Lund does not name Nye in the complaint and says nothing about Nye.

options.t: Nothing, because Rule 19(c) binds only a defendant answering a complaint.

the reasons for not joining that person

stem: Three siblings jointly hold a quarry lease. Two of them, Ortiz and Park, sue Rockline Mining for breach of the lease. The third, Quade, claims an interest in the lease but refuses to join as a plaintiff. The court finds that Quade is required to be joined, and Quade can be served and joined without any jurisdiction or venue problem.
ask: What may the court do?

options.t: Dismiss the action, because a person who refuses to join cannot be made a party.
options.why: Rule 19(a)(2) says the court must order that the person be made a party; refusal does not end the matter.

options.t: Order Quade made a party, either as a defendant or, in a proper case, as an involuntary plaintiff.
options.why: Correct. Rule 19(a)(2), second sentence.

options.t: Order Quade joined, but only as a defendant.
options.why: The rule also allows an involuntary plaintiff in a proper case.

options.t: Make Quade a party only if Rockline consents.

explain: Rule 19(a)(2) provides that if a person has not been joined as required, the court must order that the person be made a party. cites.quote: the court must order that the person be made a party. A person who refuses to join as a plaintiff may be made either a defendant or, in a proper case, an involuntary plaintiff.

stem: Singh sues Tidewater Energy on behalf of 3,000 landowners, and the court certifies the case as a class action under Rule 23. Tidewater moves to dismiss under Rule 19, arguing that every absent landowner claims an interest in the same lease payments and so must be joined individually under Rule 19(a)(1)(B).
ask: How should the court treat the argument?

options.t: Accept it: each landowner must be joined or the action dismissed under Rule 19(b).
options.why: Ignores Rule 19(d), which makes Rule 19 subject to Rule 23.

options.t: Accept it unless the class was certified under Rule 23(b)(3), the only type that overrides Rule 19.
options.why: Rule 19(d) subjects the whole rule to Rule 23 and names no particular Rule 23(b) type.

options.t: Reject it as a Rule 19 matter, because Rule 19(d) makes the rule subject to Rule 23.

stem: Reyes and Sato were both passengers on a Metro Lines bus when it collided with a truck, and each was injured. They file one complaint against Metro Lines, each alleging that the driver was negligent. Metro Lines moves to sever, arguing that two plaintiffs may not sue together without the court's permission.
ask: Are Reyes and Sato properly joined as plaintiffs?

options.t: No. Each plaintiff must first obtain leave of court before joining another plaintiff.
options.why: Rule 20(a)(1) says persons may join when its conditions are met; it requires no leave.

options.t: Yes. Their claims arise out of the same occurrence, and a common question about the driver's negligence will arise.
options.why: Correct. Rule 20(a)(1)(A) and (B) are both satisfied.

options.t: No. Joinder requires that both plaintiffs seek identical damages.
options.why: Rule 20(a)(3): a plaintiff need not be interested in all the relief demanded, so differing damages do not defeat joinder.

options.why: Rule 20(a)(1) contains no single-defendant limit.

options.t: Yes. A single plaintiff may join any defendants against whom the plaintiff has claims.
options.why: Rule 20(a)(2) imposes its own conditions on joining defendants; having claims against each is not enough.

options.why: Correct. Both conditions are required, and (A) fails.

stem: Three borrowers each signed a loan with Vance Lending during one month. Each alleges that Vance's loan officer, reading from a single written script that Vance prepared for one promotion, misstated the interest rate. The borrowers sue Vance together in one action. options.t: Yes. Each plaintiff must be interested in all the relief demanded.
options.why: Rule 20(a)(3) says the opposite.

stem: Four hundred investors have claims totaling $20 million against Norwood Fund, which holds only $2 million in assets. Early individual judgments would leave nothing for later claimants. The investors seek certification of a class because separate judgments would, as a practical matter, exhaust the fund and leave other members unable to protect their interests. Rule 23(a) is satisfied.
ask: Which Rule 23(b) subdivision fits that ground most directly?

options.t: Rule 23(b)(1)(A), because separate suits would require incompatible standards of conduct for Norwood.
options.why: Subparagraph (A) concerns inconsistent standards of conduct for the party opposing the class, not exhaustion of a fund.

options.t: Rule 23(b)(2), because Norwood acted on grounds that apply generally to the class.
options.why: Rule 23(b)(2) requires that final injunctive or declaratory relief be appropriate for the class; the investors seek no such relief.

options.t: Rule 23(b)(3), because the court must find predominance and superiority.
options.why: Those findings are the (b)(3) route; the stated ground tracks Rule 23(b)(1)(B).

options.t: Rule 23(b)(1)(B), because individual adjudications would as a practical matter be dispositive of other members' interests.
options.why: Correct. Early judgments would exhaust the fund and impair other members' ability to protect their interests.

explain: Rule 23(b)(1)(B) allows a class action when separate adjudications would, as a practical matter, be dispositive of the interests of members who are not parties to them, or would substantially impair or impede their ability to protect their interests. Early judgments exhausting the fund are exactly that risk.

cites.quote: adjudications with respect to individual class members that, as a practical matter, would be dispositive of the interests of the other members not parties to the individual adjudications or would substantially impair or impede their ability to protect their interests

stem: A class of 2,000 county jail inmates sues the Sheriff, alleging that the jail's uniform written policy of denying all inmates outdoor exercise is unlawful. The class seeks only an injunction and a declaration for the class as a whole and no money damages. The court finds that Rule 23(a) is met and that separate suits would not create the risks described in Rule 23(b)(1).
ask: Under which subdivision of Rule 23(b) may the class be maintained?

options.t: Rule 23(b)(3) only, because every class action must satisfy predominance and superiority.
options.why: Predominance and superiority are the (b)(3) findings only.

options.t: Rule 23(b)(1)(A), because every injunction creates a risk of incompatible standards.
options.why: The court found that no Rule 23(b)(1) risk exists.

options.t: Rule 23(b)(2), because the Sheriff acted on grounds that apply generally to the class and final injunctive or declaratory relief is appropriate for the class as a whole.
options.why: Correct.

options.t: None, because Rule 23(b) permits classes only for money damages.
options.why: Rule 23(b)(2) expressly covers injunctive and declaratory relief.

explain: Rule 23(b)(2) permits a class action when the party opposing the class has acted or refused to act on grounds that apply generally to the class, so that final injunctive or corresponding declaratory relief is appropriate respecting the class as a whole. A uniform jail policy challenged only for an injunction fits, and no predominance or superiority finding is needed.

cites.quote: the party opposing the class has acted or refused to act on grounds that apply generally to the class, so that final injunctive relief or corresponding declaratory relief is appropriate respecting the class as a whole

stem: Ng sues Orion Motors on behalf of 800 buyers of a car model, alleging a defective brake design. Whether the design was defective is a question common to all buyers, but each buyer would have to prove separate facts about whether the brakes failed, when, and what repairs cost. The court finds that those individual questions would dominate the case. Rule 23(a) is satisfied.
ask: May the class be certified under Rule 23(b)(3)?

options.t: No. The court cannot find that common questions predominate over individual ones, which Rule 23(b)(3) requires.
options.why: Correct.

options.t: Yes. A common question under Rule 23(a)(2) already supplies predominance.
options.why: Rule 23(a)(2) commonality and Rule 23(b)(3) predominance are separate requirements.

options.t: Yes, because the class is large.
options.why: Size bears on Rule 23(a)(1) numerosity, not predominance.

options.t: No, because Rule 23(b)(3) classes may not include members with damages claims.
options.why: Rule 23(b)(3) imposes no such bar.

explain: Rule 23(b)(3) requires the court to find that questions common to class members predominate over questions affecting only individual members, and that a class action is superior to other methods. stem: A court is deciding whether to certify a Rule 23(b)(3) class of 5,000 purchasers of Zeta Appliances. It learns that 300 class members have already filed individual lawsuits against Zeta over the same product in other courts, and several are near trial. The judge asks which of the pertinent matters listed in Rule 23(b)(3) addresses suits already begun by class members.
ask: Which listed matter is that?

options.t: Rule 23(b)(3)(A): class members' interests in individually controlling separate actions.
options.why: That factor addresses members' interest in control, not the extent and nature of litigation already begun.

options.t: Rule 23(b)(3)(B): the extent and nature of any litigation concerning the controversy already begun by class members.
options.why: Correct.

options.t: Rule 23(b)(3)(C): the desirability of concentrating the litigation in the particular forum.
options.why: That factor concerns the choice of forum, not suits already begun.

options.t: Rule 23(b)(3)(D): the likely difficulties in managing a class action.
options.why: That factor concerns manageability.

explain: Rule 23(b)(3)(B) lists as pertinent to the predominance and superiority findings the extent and nature of any litigation concerning the controversy already begun by or against class members. The 300 pending individual suits are litigation already begun by class members.

cites.quote: the extent and nature of any litigation concerning the controversy already begun by or against class members

stem: The court certifies a class of 5,000 under Rule 23(b)(3). Zeta's own records give mailing addresses for 4,800 of the members. Class counsel proposes only a posting on a website, and the judge notes that it would be the cheapest way to give notice.
ask: May the court limit notice to the website posting?

options.t: Yes. Notice to a certified class is always discretionary: the court 'may' direct it.
options.why: Discretionary notice applies to Rule 23(b)(1) and (b)(2) classes under Rule 23(c)(2)(A); (b)(3) notice is mandatory.

options.t: Yes, if the posting states the class definition in plain language.
options.why: Plain language is required, but the manner must also be the best notice practicable.

options.t: No. Individual notice is required only for members who request exclusion.
options.why: Rule 23(c)(2)(B) requires individual notice to all members identifiable through reasonable effort.

options.t: No. The court must direct the best notice practicable, including individual notice to all members who can be identified through reasonable effort.
options.why: Correct. Rule 23(c)(2)(B).

explain: For a Rule 23(b)(3) class, Rule 23(c)(2)(B) requires the best notice practicable under the circumstances, including individual notice to all members identifiable through reasonable effort, by mail, electronic means or other appropriate means. Zeta's records identify 4,800 members, so a website posting alone is insufficient.

cites.quote: the court must direct to class members the best notice that is practicable under the circumstances, including individual notice to all members who can be identified through reasonable effort
the court may direct appropriate notice to the class

stem: Hana sues Brightline Utilities on behalf of 10,000 customers charged an unlawful surcharge on one bill. She seeks only money damages; Brightline has ended the practice, and no injunction or declaration is sought. The court finds that joinder of 10,000 customers is impracticable and that the surcharge raises common questions. Brightline is solvent, so no limited fund exists. No settlement has been proposed. The judge asks which provisions govern the certification decision and its timing.
ask: Which provisions apply? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 23(a)(1)
options.why: Joinder of 10,000 customers is impracticable.

options.t: Rule 23(a)(2)
options.why: The surcharge raises questions common to the class.

options.t: Rule 23(b)(2)
options.why: No injunction or declaration is sought, so final injunctive or declaratory relief is not at issue.

options.t: Rule 23(b)(3)
options.why: A damages class requires findings of predominance and superiority.

options.t: Rule 23(c)(1)(A)
options.why: The court must decide whether to certify at an early practicable time after the suit is filed.

options.t: Rule 23(c)(2)(A)
options.why: Discretionary notice covers (b)(1) and (b)(2) classes; this class would be a (b)(3) class.

options.t: Rule 23(e)
options.why: No settlement, dismissal or compromise has been proposed.

explain: Numerosity (23(a)(1)) and commonality (23(a)(2)) are found, and a damages-only class fits 23(b)(3). The court must decide certification at an early practicable time (23(c)(1)(A)). the court finds that the questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members

stem: A Rule 23(b)(3) class was certified against Kiln Products a year ago. The parties now propose a settlement that would bind the class. Under a side agreement, class counsel would pay objector Bale $20,000 to withdraw his objection to the settlement. The agreement has not been disclosed to the court. No one is appealing any certification order, and attorney's fees have not yet been addressed.
ask: Which provisions apply? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 23(c)(1)(A)
options.why: The class was certified a year ago, so the timing of the certification decision is not at issue.

options.t: Rule 23(e)(2)
options.why: A proposal that would bind class members may be approved only after a hearing and a finding that it is fair, reasonable, and adequate.

options.t: Rule 23(e)(3)
options.why: The parties must file a statement identifying any agreement made in connection with the proposal.

options.t: Rule 23(e)(5)(B)
options.why: No payment may be provided in connection with withdrawing an objection unless the court approves after a hearing.

options.t: Rule 23(f)
options.why: No one is petitioning to appeal a certification order.

options.t: Rule 23(h)
options.why: No motion for attorney's fees has been made.

explain: The settlement would bind the class, so it needs a hearing and a fair, reasonable and adequate finding (23(e)(2)). The Bale side agreement must be identified in a statement filed with the court (23(e)(3)), and the $20,000 payment for withdrawing the objection needs approval after a hearing (23(e)(5)(B)). Certification timing, appeals and fees are not in play.
